Temperature inversions

Source: R/apx.R
invsn.Rd

The instrument of Bondy, Roth and Sager (2020, p. 566-567): "the continuous difference between temperatures at the ground level and temperatures at circa 750 m altitude (925 hectopascals (hPa) pressure level)". On most days the air cools with height; in an inversion it is warmer above than at the ground, and pollutants are trapped near the ground.

Usage

invsn(
  tlow,
  tup,
  sign = c("upper", "ground"),
  brk = NULL,
  by = NULL,
  rule = c("all", "any", "mean")
)

Arguments

tlow

Temperatures at the ground (numbers, NA allowed).

tup

Temperatures aloft, at the same places and times, in the same unit.

sign

"upper" or "ground": which temperature comes first.

brk

NULL or the breaks of the bins of the difference (as in cut(), right-closed).

by

NULL or the group of each reading (a day, say): one row per group, as below.

rule

With by, when a group is an inversion: "all" (every reading with both temperatures inverted), "any" or "mean" (the mean difference above 0). Cautions from a review of 81 studies that use the instrument (Yamada 2026, section 7 and table 8, pp. 24-25), whose nine checks the help here follows. The instrument's strong first stages, mostly from China, do not carry over: in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia definitions drawn from published practice gave first stages that were strong yet second stages of opposite sign, and an inversion day moved PM2.5 by about one microgram per cubic metre, small beside the direct effects of the cold, still weather that comes with it, so the exclusion restriction fails through weather and season. The checks: (1) the reference layers must lie above ground everywhere in the study area; (2) the temperatures should be taken at local dawn; (3) report the share of zeros and the support of the instrument (the diag attribute of the result gives them); (4) estimate with both a pressure-level and a surface-layer definition and report both; (5) report the first stage in physical units relative to the mean exposure, not only its F (the fstab table of ivfe()); (6) where two definitions are available, test them against each other (an over-identification test across them; not computed here); (7) run a placebo outcome without a pollution pathway (any outcome in ivfe() or ppmlcf()); (8) check robustness to place-by-month fixed effects; (9) validate the exposure against ground monitors at the scale of the contrasts used.

Value

A data frame: diff, the difference by sign; inv, 1 when tup is above tlow and 0 otherwise (NA where a temperature is missing); and with brk, bin, a factor. With by, one row per group, sorted: by, n (the readings with both temperatures), diff (their mean difference), inv (by rule; NA without a reading) and bin. The attribute "diag" is a one-row data frame: n, the rows (groups) with both temperatures; zero, the share of them without an inversion; min, max, the support of diff.

Details

The choices. The paper does not say which temperature is subtracted from which: sign = "upper" (the default) gives the upper temperature less the ground one, positive in an inversion; sign = "ground" the reverse, as the paper's words run. inv is 1 in an inversion (upper warmer than ground) whatever the sign; the indicator, rather than the continuous difference, is the other common form of the instrument. With brk, bin gives the strength in bins of the difference (by the chosen sign), for an instrument that lets weak and strong inversions act differently.

From readings to days (by, rule). Batkeyev and DeRemer (2023, sec. 4.3, p. 297) compare a station at the city's elevation with one in its high southeast corner, read every three hours, and define "a dummy which equals 1 if within a day all low-elevation temperature readings are less than high-elevation temperature readings" (by the day, rule = "all", the default), a demanding standard that still finds inversions on more than 35% of their days; where evening readings were missing they use the readings there are, as "all" does here. "any" and "mean" are weaker rules, and diff (the mean difference) is the continuous form of their appendix (sec. A3). Their other instrument, the share of a period's readings with the wind from the mountains (from the southeast, south-by-southeast or east-by-southeast, 101.25 to 168.75 degrees), set to 0 for the districts far from the mountains, is windiv() with sect = c(101.25, 168.75), by the period and share = TRUE.

Cautions. Inversions cover large areas (the paper's satellite readings are on a grid of about 110 by 70 km), so they vary little between places in a city; Bondy, Roth and Sager use them at the borough and city level and report a weaker first stage there than for wind (their table 5). As an instrument the inversion must affect the outcome only through the exposure; inversions come with cold, still, clear weather, which may change what people do as well, so weather controls matter (see ivfe()).

References

Bondy, M., Roth, S. and Sager, L. (2020). Crime is in the air: the contemporaneous relationship between air pollution and crime. Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists, 7(3), 555-585. doi:10.1086/707127

Yamada, H. (2026). When the air doesn't move the data: the thermal inversion instrument in developing countries. Keio-IES Discussion Paper DP2026-018, Keio University.

Batkeyev, B. and DeRemer, D. R. (2023). Mountains of evidence: the effects of abnormal air pollution on crime. Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization, 210, 288-319. doi:10.1016/j.jebo.2023.04.009

See also

windiv(), ivfe(), ppmlcf()

Examples

invsn(c(10, 5, 2), c(8, 6, 2))
#>   diff inv
#> 1   -2   0
#> 2    1   1
#> 3    0   0
# three-hourly readings, one row per day: inverted when every reading is
invsn(c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3), c(4, 5, 6, 4, 1, 6), by = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2))
#>   by n     diff inv
#> 1  1 3 3.000000   1
#> 2  2 3 1.666667   0
invsn(c(10, 5, 2), c(8, 6, 2), sign = "ground", brk = c(-Inf, -1, 0, Inf))
#>   diff inv       bin
#> 1    2   0  (0, Inf]
#> 2   -1   1 (-Inf,-1]
#> 3    0   0    (-1,0]
# the share of days without an inversion and the support (check 3)
attr(invsn(c(10, 5, 2), c(8, 6, 2)), "diag")
#>   n      zero min max
#> 1 3 0.6666667  -2   1
